title: pulse recovery supervisor: apply repo-declared recovery policy (outlier hold, session-cap split, pre-authorized brief repair)
body:
## What

Let a repo declare its own queue-recovery policy, and let the pulse terminal-blocker / integration-recovery supervisor apply it as delegated authority. Three actions are in scope:

- **Exhausted-outlier hold**: when an issue's recorded evidence shows every acquisition path failed (or programme identity is unresolved after the checkpoint), apply `hold-for-review` across the issue's dependency chain. Post one decision comment with the evidence and reopen conditions, plus pointer comments on the rest of the chain. Then repoint any dependant whose scope is independent of the held issue onto the held issue's own completed predecessor, so the rest of the queue keeps moving.
- **Session-cap split**: when an issue has used the repo's declared session budget, has an unfinished ledger, and its partial PR has merged, file one worker-ready split task. Use the repo's declared split pattern and template. Then block the issue on that task instead of redispatching it.
- **Brief authority repair**: when `files_scope_excluded` or `input_required` names a boundary that the repo policy pre-authorizes (for example "a later phase may add minimal source-backed records the earlier phase left empty"), apply the brief repair and release the issue.

## Evidence (managed private repo, one manual triage session, 2026-10-19)

A maintainer applied exactly these actions by hand, guided by the repo's documented policy:

- 3 award chains held as exhausted outliers. One source returned HTTP 403 to browser capture and a page shell to the approved provider; one had unresolved programme identity; one was a paywalled archive. Each had already gone through 6–7 dispatches ending `input_required` or `files_scope_excluded`.
- 1 dependant repointed around a held part, so a sibling part became dispatchable.
- 3 issues routed to split tasks after exhausting their session budget. They had been sitting at `status:in-review` or `status:available` with no `auto-dispatch`.
- 1 brief repaired: a results phase was blocked because the core phase closed with zero stored editions, and the repo policy allows the later phase to add minimal edition records.

`pulse-wrapper-cycle.sh` (around line 222) currently tells the supervisor to "repair brief or environment defects within existing authority, never grant permissions". It has no way to learn repo-specific queue policy, so these cases wait for a human even when the repo has already decided the rule.

## How

1. Add an optional `.aidevops.json` key, `recovery_policy`, that points to a repo document section. The document lists the enabled actions (`outlier_hold`, `session_cap_split`, `brief_authority`), each with its conditions, an issue template, and labels.
2. In the terminal-blocker recovery supervisor prompt (`pulse-wrapper-cycle.sh`) and `reference/worker-discipline.md` "Terminal-blocker recovery", load that section as evidence of maintainer-delegated authority. Treat only enabled actions as authorized. Record each application through `terminal-blocker-recovery-helper.sh record` with `wake=human_decision` (holds) or `wake=dependency_change` (splits and repoints).
3. Keep every existing safety rule: no credentials, permissions, data imports, record merges or publication. A hold is reversible and stays labelled.
4. Recovery queues are runner-local today. Also let any runner with maintainer access apply policy actions to circuits opened elsewhere, using only public issue and PR evidence, so one offline runner can't strand its circuits.

## Verification

- Add `tests/test-terminal-blocker-circuit.sh` cases (or a new supervisor-policy test):
  - With no `recovery_policy`, behaviour is unchanged.
  - With `outlier_hold` enabled, a fixture issue whose evidence names both failed acquisition paths gets the hold, decision comment and dependant repoint.
  - An action not listed in the policy isn't applied.
- Run ShellCheck on the touched scripts.

title: headless workers: read-wide, write-narrow — read-only sibling worktrees, read-only toolchain roots, canonical-checkout redirect
body:
## What

Give headless workers a read-wide, write-narrow filesystem boundary:

1. **Sibling worktrees become read-only for workers.** A headless worker may read anything under the worktree base, but `edit`, `write` and `apply_patch` (and mutating `git -C <path>` commands) may only target its own `WORKER_WORKTREE_PATH`, plus managed temp under `AIDEVOPS_TEMP_DIR`.
2. **Read-only toolchain roots are allowed without a maintainer.** Allow `read`/`glob`/`grep`/`list` (never writes) under `~/.nvm/**`, still filtered by the broker's `FORBIDDEN_PATTERN`.
3. **Canonical checkout requests get an owned redirect instead of a maintainer hold:** "read the same tracked path in your own worktree; install dependencies worktree-locally." The canonical checkout stays non-grantable to workers.

Interactive sessions are unchanged. Cross-repository linked-worktree writes stay allowed there, as `tests/test-git-safety-gate.mjs` ("allows cross-repository linked writes only inside the trusted Git workspace") asserts.

## Why

- **Workers can currently write to other workers' worktrees.** Both permission generators allow the whole worktree base: `.agents/scripts/lib/agent_config.py` `managed_external_directories()` (around line 63) and `.agents/scripts/generate-runtime-config-agents.sh` (around lines 431–432). An OpenCode `external_directory: allow` covers writes as well as reads, and `quality-hooks-git-safety.mjs` doesn't fence headless writes to `WORKER_WORKTREE_PATH`. A confused worker could therefore edit or commit in a concurrent worker's checkout. Reading other worktrees is useful (salvaging prepared files from stale drafts, comparing approaches). Writing to them is never part of a worker's job.
- **Permission-request evidence.** I scanned 51 issues in one managed repo that carried "Maintainer permission required" comments:
  - 26 were read-only `~/.nvm/*` requests, each pausing a worker for a maintainer.
  - 28 targeted the canonical checkout (22 via bash, 6 via read).

title: Playwright MCP native tool filenames resolve against the client root and write into canonical checkouts (GH#34111 gap)
body:
## Observed failure (follow-up to GH#34111)

On 2026-10-15 an interactive OpenCode session delegated a read-only dark-mode check to a `playwright` subagent. The prompt said screenshots may only go under `~/.aidevops/.agent-workspace/tmp/`. The child called `playwright_browser_take_screenshot` with `filename: "<name>.png"` (a bare relative name), twice. Both images, viewport screenshots of a client's website, were written to the root of the **canonical checkout** of an unrelated plugin repository: the session's project directory. The child then searched the MCP session artifact folder, could not find the files and reported "could not verify either as a file". The parent did not check `git status`.

The files stayed there for 4 days. Every canonical fast-forward in that time (41 merges) made a new dirty-worktree backup holding the same two untracked images: 41 `refs/aidevops/dirty-worktree-backups/*` refs in the project repository plus 41 copies under `tmp/dirty-main-backups/`. Nothing alerted the owner, who found them in a session's closing `git status`. Nothing was pushed: origin had only heads, tags and PR refs.

Earlier dirty backups for other repositories show the same pattern (an untracked `.playwright-mcp/` folder, and many `*-desktop.png`, `*-mobile.png` or `*-dark.png` files in canonical roots), so this was not a one-off.

## Root cause (verified in source)

GH#34111 made the Playwright MCP process start in a private per-session folder (`mcp-registry.mjs` launcher: `cd -- "$output_dir"; exec "$@" --output-dir "$output_dir"`; `browser-mcp-launcher.sh` likewise). That covers raw `page.screenshot({path})` in run-code. It does **not** cover the `filename` argument of the native tools, because `@playwright/mcp@0.0.79` (`playwright-core/lib/coreBundle.js`) resolves those against the **MCP client root**, not the process cwd and not `--output-dir`:

- `initializeServer`: when the client advertises the `roots` capability, `clientInfo.cwd = firstRootPath(await server.listRoots())`; it falls back to `process.cwd()` only when there are no roots (`allRootPaths`, ~l.71524).
- `Response.resolveClientFile` → `resolveClientFilename(filename)` → `workspaceFile(options, fileName, this._clientWorkspace)` → `path.resolve(options.cwd, fileName)` (~l.64699, 65204-65216).
- `checkFile` allows any path inside `outputDir` **or** the client workspace (~l.64720), so the write is allowed.

OpenCode advertises the session's project directory as the root, so `filename: "x.png"` lands in `<project>/x.png`. Screenshots without `filename` go to `--output-dir` as expected. The comment above the `playwright` registry entry ("explicit relative output filenames remaining within that directory") is incorrect for 0.0.79. The same resolution applies to `browser_snapshot`, `browser_pdf_save`, storage-state, video and response-body `filename`s.

## Proposed fix

1. **Runtime confinement (primary).** In the Playwright launch path, put a minimal stdio JSON-RPC filter between client and server that removes `params.capabilities.roots` from the client's `initialize` request, and does not forward `roots/list` or `notifications/roots/list_changed`. Playwright then falls back to `process.cwd()`, which is already the private artifact folder, so every relative `filename` lands under the session's artifact root. No CLI option exists for this (`allowUnrestrictedFileAccess` widens access instead). Keep the pinned version and the `mcp-diagnose.sh` version check working. Correct the registry comment.
2. **Surface stray artifacts instead of re-backing them up silently.** When the canonical fast-forward or recovery path finds untracked files that byte-match an existing open or acknowledged backup, do not make another backup. Raise one actionable owner notice (session greeting or pulse) listing the paths, and offer the existing verified `clean` path. Untracked media (`*.png|jpg|webp|pdf|webm`) or `.playwright-mcp/` at a canonical root should be classed as likely agent artifacts in that notice.
3. **Delegation guard.** After a browser-capable child (`playwright`, `playwriter`, `chrome-devtools`) returns, have the parent or plugin compare `git status --porcelain` of the session directory before and after the call. Report any new untracked paths in the child's result. Update `tools/browser/browser-automation.md` and `workflows/ui-verification.md`: until (1) ships, omit `filename` on native screenshot tools (or give an absolute path inside the reported output dir), and a child that "cannot find" its screenshot must check the project directory.

## Files to modify

- `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/mcp-registry.mjs`: the Playwright launcher (~l.776-805) and the registry comment (~l.439).
- `.agents/scripts/browser-mcp-launcher.sh`: the same filter for the non-plugin config path.
- `.agents/scripts/canonical-recovery-helper.sh` and/or `.agents/scripts/dirty-worktree-backup-helper.sh`: dedupe identical untracked payloads; owner notice.
- `.agents/tools/browser/browser-automation.md`, `.agents/workflows/ui-verification.md`: guidance.
- Tests next to the existing launcher/registry tests (discover their exact paths; do not guess).

## Verification

- In a disposable Git repository opened as the OpenCode project, call `browser_take_screenshot` with `filename: "probe.png"`, with no filename, and run-code `page.screenshot({path: "./probe2.png"})`. All three files are under the per-session artifact root; `git status --porcelain` of the project is empty; the tool's printable link still reads back.
- `browser_snapshot` with `filename` behaves the same.
- A canonical fast-forward with a stray untracked image creates at most one backup, and a second fast-forward makes no new backup but raises one notice.
- `mcp-diagnose.sh check-all` still reports the pinned Playwright version.

This brief omits project identity, customer content and private paths.

title: OpenCode 2: gpt_image_generate OAuth always fails — v2.mjs does not pass imageOAuthAccountResolver to createTools
body:
## Summary

On OpenCode 2, `gpt_image_generate` with the default `auth: "oauth"` always fails with:

```
OpenAI OAuth account selection is unavailable in this runtime.
```

even when the OpenAI OAuth pool has an active account.

## Cause

`createTools()` (`plugins/opencode-aidevops/tools.mjs`) passes `options.imageOAuthAccountResolver` / `imageOAuthAccountRotator` / `imageFetch` into `createGptImageTool()`. `gpt-image-auth.mjs` `resolveOAuthAuth()` throws when the resolver is not a function.

- `index.mjs` (OpenCode 1) passes `imageFetch`, `imageOAuthAccountResolver: selectOpenAIRequestAccount` and `imageOAuthAccountRotator`.
- `v2.mjs` (OpenCode 2) calls `createTools(SCRIPTS_DIR, run, {...})` without any of the three, so the OAuth path can never work on OpenCode 2.

## Environment

- aidevops 3.39.47
- OpenCode Desktop 2.0.28 (macOS), plugin loaded via `v2.mjs`

## Local workaround (verified offline)

In `v2.mjs`, import `selectOpenAIRequestAccount` from `./oauth-pool.mjs` and add to the `createTools` options:

```js
imageFetch: globalThis.fetch?.bind(globalThis),
imageOAuthAccountResolver: selectOpenAIRequestAccount,
```

With that, `resolveGptImageAuth({ auth: "oauth" }, { resolveOAuthAccount: selectOpenAIRequestAccount })` returns `mode: "oauth"` with the pooled account.

The rotator was deliberately left out: `rotateOpenAIPoolToken()` → `applyOpenAIPoolAccount()` rewrites `process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY` and calls `client.auth.set`, which is the OpenCode 1 provider-auth path and may conflict with `v2-provider-auth.mjs`. An OpenCode 2-safe rotator (select next pool account without mutating provider auth) would be the full fix.

## Suggested fix

Pass an image OAuth resolver (and an OpenCode 2-safe rotator) from `v2.mjs`, and add an OpenCode 2 wiring test alongside `tests/test-gpt-image-tool.mjs`.
